paragraphs: This paper asks whether simple statistics of image contrast capture information people use to recognize a scene at a glance. Contrast patterns in most natural images follow a Weibull distribution. The researchers use this regularity to build a model linking image statistics to measured brain responses, testing whether those statistics convey a scene’s overall visual character.

During a learning phase, 32 participants viewed brief presentations of 800 natural scenes while their EEG activity was recorded. The researchers combined these measurements with the images’ contrast statistics to construct a response model across participants. For new scenes, the model predicted EEG responses; identification then involved matching those predictions against the response actually observed.

The model identified the viewed scene in almost 90 percent of cases. When it failed, the selected scene was usually visually similar to the actual one. Together, these findings suggest that Weibull contrast statistics retain substantial information about scene gist. They support the usefulness of this statistical representation for rapid identification without establishing that it fully explains human scene recognition.
neurips-2009-a-biologically-plausible-mo.tldr: A model linking natural-image contrast statistics to EEG responses identified viewed scenes in almost 90 percent of cases.

paragraphs: In stochastic control, a cost-to-go function describes the future cost associated with a situation. Approximating this function is central to dynamic programming when the problem has many dimensions. This paper introduces a linear programming formulation that changes a restriction imposed by existing linear programming approaches: their approximations are constrained to lie below the optimal cost-to-go function.

The proposed smoothed approximate linear program relaxes that lower-bound requirement while preserving computational tractability. This gives the approximation more freedom in how it represents future costs. The contribution concerns both the optimization formulation and its analysis: the authors establish improved bounds on approximation quality, providing theoretical support for allowing this additional flexibility.

The authors also test the method on Tetris, a challenging control problem. They report performance an order of magnitude better than the existing linear programming approach, which had previously been competitive with several approximate dynamic programming algorithms. This experimental result supports the proposed relaxation in that setting, while the improved approximation bounds provide a separate mathematical reason to consider the formulation.
neurips-2009-a-smoothed-approximate-line.tldr: Relaxing a lower-bound constraint yields a tractable linear program with improved approximation bounds and substantially better reported Tetris performance.

paragraphs: Estimating a model with many parameters requires assumptions about its structure. Examples include sparsity, where relatively few parameters matter, and low rank in matrix-valued parameters. Regularized M-estimation combines a loss measuring agreement with the data and a penalty encouraging the chosen structure. This paper develops a common framework for analyzing the accuracy of these procedures.

The main contribution is a theorem giving convergence rates measured in any metric norm. Such rates describe how estimation error changes as information accumulates. Applying the same theorem lets the authors recover existing results and derive a range of new ones, bringing analyses of different structured estimation problems into a shared mathematical framework.

The analysis highlights restricted strong convexity of the loss and decomposability of the regularizer as key properties supporting good convergence rates. These properties connect the behavior of the fitting objective with the structure encouraged by the penalty. The practical significance is analytical: researchers can examine these common conditions when studying an estimator instead of developing an entirely separate argument for every formulation.
neurips-2009-a-unified-framework-for-hig.tldr: A unified theorem establishes convergence rates for structured regularized estimators and identifies loss and penalty properties that support accurate estimation.

paragraphs: Transparent objects are difficult to recognize from local image features because their appearance strongly reflects what lies behind them. A patch on glass or plastic contains background structure modified by refraction, and the background often dominates. Consequently, matching patches to individual examples or assigning them to conventional visual codewords can miss patterns characteristic of transparency.

The paper models a transparent patch as an additive combination of hidden factors. Some account for background scene content; others capture the distribution of local edge energy associated with refraction. Its LDA-SIFT formulation applies LDA before vector quantization, discovering latent topics associated with transparent patches. Those topic dimensions then guide the construction of transparent visual words.

This ordering matters because the representation can account for mixed background and refraction contributions before compressing local features into discrete categories. The method requires no knowledge of the background scene at test time. The authors demonstrate examples of recognizing transparent glasses in a domestic environment, illustrating how the learned representation can support recognition when background appearance is a major part of the observed object.
neurips-2009-an-additive-latent-feature-.tldr: An additive latent-feature representation separates background and refraction contributions to support transparent-object recognition without knowing the test-time background.

paragraphs: Maximum a posteriori inference seeks the most probable joint configuration in a probabilistic graphical model. This paper approaches approximation by first simplifying the model’s structure. The simplified model provides a starting point from which the method identifies what the relaxation fails to capture and introduces compensation for those deficiencies.

This perspective separates two kinds of approximation according to the idealized conditions used to guide compensation. The authors show that max-product belief propagation can be understood as compensating for a structural relaxation under one particular idealized case of exactness. A more refined idealized case motivates a second compensation approach, producing a new approximation with different properties.

The paper also proposes a class of algorithms that progressively tighten an initial relaxation. This makes approximation a process of controlled refinement rather than a single fixed simplification. The conceptual contribution is to connect an established inference method and a new alternative through the same relaxation-and-compensation framework. Exactness remains tied to the idealized cases used in the analysis; the general algorithms are presented as producing increasingly tight approximations.
neurips-2009-approximating-map-by-compen.tldr: Viewing MAP approximation as structural simplification followed by compensation connects max-product belief propagation with new, progressively tighter inference methods.

paragraphs: Minimum Description Length chooses a model by balancing the code needed to describe the model against the code needed to describe the data under it. This paper investigates the predictive consequences of that selection rule. Its central result concerns a countable collection of candidate models that contains the true data-generating probability measure.

Under that setting, the predictions of models selected by MDL, or by MAP, asymptotically merge with the true measure in total variation distance. Total variation measures discrepancies across events, so this is a strong form of predictive agreement. The conclusion concerns predictions becoming accurate over time, without requiring that model selection settle on a uniquely identifiable explanation.

The theorem does not require independence, stationarity, ergodicity, or identifiability assumptions on the model class. That breadth makes it relevant to settings where observations have dependencies or their distribution changes over time. The paper discusses implications for time-series forecasting, discriminative learning, and reinforcement learning. The essential qualifications are that the candidate class is countable, includes the true measure, and the predictive guarantee is asymptotic.
neurips-2009-discrete-mdl-predicts-in-to.tldr: For a countable model class containing the truth, MDL or MAP predictions converge to the true measure in total variation without independence or stationarity assumptions.

paragraphs: Hierarchical classification organizes labels within a taxonomy, making the hierarchy part of how prediction errors are judged. This paper questions how that judgment should be defined. Taxonomies reflect many arbitrary design decisions and are often unbalanced, so their structure can influence the loss assigned to a prediction in ways that warrant correction.

The authors propose calibrating the classification loss using the data distribution. This leads to a revised definition of statistical risk, the expected loss that a learning method aims to control. Incorporating distributional information requires care because the correction can create difficult statistical dependencies. The proposed analysis therefore moves from binomial-type estimation to a geometric-type approach.

The resulting contributions are a calibrated risk definition, an unbiased geometric estimator of that risk, and a reduction to cost-sensitive classification. Unbiasedness means the estimator targets the defined risk correctly in expectation. The reduction connects the revised objective to a classification setting that explicitly handles different error costs. Together, these results address both what hierarchical classification should optimize and how that objective can be estimated and pursued.
neurips-2009-distribution-calibrated-hie.tldr: The paper calibrates hierarchical classification loss to the data distribution and supplies an unbiased risk estimator and a cost-sensitive learning reduction.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines several kernels when the most suitable feature representation is unclear. Earlier approaches encourage sparse combinations, which make the selected kernels easier to interpret. The paper points out that L1-based multiple kernel learning has rarely surpassed simple baselines in practical applications, motivating a broader family of ways to combine kernels.

The authors generalize the formulation to arbitrary Lp norms, allowing mixtures that need not be sparse. They also clarify connections among existing formulations and develop two interleaved optimization strategies for p greater than one. These strategies address the computational side of learning a kernel mixture, making the broader formulation practical to optimize.

Experiments show that the interleaved strategies are much faster than the wrapper approaches traditionally used for this task. On real computational biology problems, the authors report that non-sparse mixtures exceed the state-of-the-art accuracy. These findings support retaining contributions from multiple kernels in the evaluated settings and show that the choice of sparsity preference and optimization strategy both matter for practical multiple kernel learning.
neurips-2009-efficient-and-accurate-lp-n.tldr: Lp-norm multiple kernel learning enables non-sparse mixtures, with faster reported optimization and improved accuracy on computational biology tasks.

paragraphs: Training conditional maximum entropy models on very large datasets can demand substantial computing time and resources. This paper studies how distributing the training work changes those costs. It compares three common strategies: distributing gradient computation, combining predictions through majority voting, and combining the parameters of independently trained models.

These strategies combine work at different levels. Distributed gradients contribute to optimization, voting combines model decisions, and parameter mixtures combine learned model parameters. The authors analyze worst-case runtime and resource requirements for all three approaches. They identify parameter mixtures as the most efficient strategy in this comparison and provide a theoretical foundation for convergence of the resulting parameters.

Large-scale experiments compare the approaches and show that mixtures of independent models use fewer resources while obtaining comparable loss to standard methods. The result matters because it connects computational savings with the quality of the trained model: efficiency is evaluated alongside loss. The paper thus supports parameter mixing as an effective distributed training strategy in the studied setting, with both a cost analysis and convergence theory behind the empirical comparison.
neurips-2009-efficient-large-scale-distr.tldr: Combining independently trained model parameters uses fewer resources while achieving comparable loss in large-scale conditional maximum entropy experiments.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a viewed image from brain activity requires a representation of the image and a mapping from neural measurements to that representation. Earlier work used fixed image bases at several scales and learned how fMRI responses predicted their contrasts. This paper asks whether the image bases themselves can instead be learned from the measured data.

The authors build a probabilistic model connecting fMRI activity and visual images through latent variables. The mapping from those hidden variables into image space acts as the set of image bases. Learning this mapping allows the reconstruction model to discover its visual building blocks together with their relationship to brain activity, rather than fixing their shapes in advance.

The estimated bases near the fovea were spatially localized and appeared at multiple scales. Using these learned bases, the model accurately reconstructed novel visual images. These findings show that a useful reconstruction representation can emerge from the measured brain–image relationship. The method also provides a way to investigate functional mappings between visual stimuli and neural activity through the image structures it learns.
neurips-2009-estimating-image-bases-for-.tldr: A probabilistic model learns image bases from fMRI and visual data, discovering localized multiscale structure and accurately reconstructing novel images.

paragraphs: Multiple-object tracking experiments examine how people maintain attention to several moving objects. Failures are often attributed to specialized cognitive systems with limited capacity. This paper separates two possible sources of difficulty: limitations in cognition and uncertainty inherent in the visual information available during tracking. That distinction matters because uncertain observations can cause errors even for a principled observer.

The authors analyze tracking with a dynamic probabilistic model and use a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter as their ideal observer. They compare its behavior with human performance measured in new behavioral experiments. Many observed patterns of human success and failure arise naturally from the model’s operation, showing that perceptual uncertainty can account for substantial aspects of tracking behavior.

One pattern requires an additional explanation: the tradeoff between how fast objects move and how many can be tracked. The analysis attributes this tradeoff to allocation of a flexible cognitive resource, formalizable as memory or attention. The resulting account combines uncertainty-based inference with resource constraints, distinguishing the phenomena explained by the observation problem from those requiring a cognitive capacity component.
neurips-2009-explaining-human-multiple-o.tldr: A probabilistic observer explains many human tracking phenomena, while the speed–object-count tradeoff requires a flexible cognitive resource in the analysis.

paragraphs: This paper combines information from classifiers and clustering methods to assign labels jointly to a collection of objects. Classifiers provide predicted labels, while clustering outputs provide constraints about which objects belong together. Combining both can broaden an ensemble’s information sources, including situations where only model outputs are available and the underlying raw data cannot be accessed.

The authors formulate consensus as an optimization problem on a bipartite graph. The objective encourages neighboring nodes to have smooth conditional probability estimates while penalizing departures from the initial supervised labels. Iterative propagation passes these estimates among neighboring nodes, seeking a globally coordinated assignment rather than deciding every object’s label through a separate majority vote.

The method also admits interpretations as constrained embedding in a transformed space and as ranking on a graph. These viewpoints connect the label-combination procedure to the structure of its optimization. Experiments on three real applications demonstrate benefits over existing alternatives. The contribution is a concrete way to make supervised predictions and unsupervised grouping information jointly influence classification through a shared consensus objective.
neurips-2009-graph-based-consensus-maxim.tldr: A graph-based optimization combines classifier predictions and clustering constraints into joint labels, with reported benefits on three real applications.

paragraphs: In some regression problems, explanatory variables come in natural groups. Selecting variables one at a time can fail to respect that organization. This paper studies how to choose groups for least-squares regression and proposes Group Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, or Group-OMP, as an efficient greedy method that incorporates the grouping directly into selection.

Group-OMP extends ordinary Orthogonal Matching Pursuit from stage-wise selection of individual variables to stage-wise selection of groups. The authors prove that the procedure can recover the correct variable groups under certain conditions. They also bound the infinity-norm difference between estimated and true regression coefficients, which controls the largest absolute error among the coefficients.

Experiments on simulated and real datasets compare Group-OMP with Group Lasso, ordinary OMP, and Lasso. The reported results are favorable for both variable selection and prediction accuracy. The paper therefore connects a simple group-aware selection procedure with conditional recovery guarantees and empirical evidence. Its theoretical claim is specifically that correct recovery holds under the stated conditions, while its experimental findings describe performance on the datasets evaluated.
neurips-2009-grouped-orthogonal-matching.tldr: Group-OMP greedily selects variable groups, with conditional recovery guarantees, coefficient-error bounds, and favorable reported regression results.

paragraphs: Synaptic strengths and release probabilities change over short timescales, which can look like unwanted variability if a synapse is assumed to perform a fixed operation. This paper proposes a computational purpose for that flexibility. A neuron’s spikes provide only an incomplete report of its continuously varying membrane potential, leaving receiving synapses with an estimation problem.

The theory suggests that a synapse combines incoming spikes with prior expectations to estimate the presynaptic membrane potential, much like a recursive filter. The authors show that the characteristic dynamics of short-term synaptic depression closely resemble those required for optimal estimation and can support high-quality estimates. This gives synaptic changes a role in extracting information from incomplete signals.

Within this account, the local postsynaptic potential and available synaptic resources track scaled versions of the estimated mean and variance of the presynaptic potential. The theory also yields experimentally testable predictions connecting subthreshold fluctuations and the form of spike generation to short-term plasticity in particular cell types. These are proposed functional relationships and predictions of the account, rather than reported experimental confirmation of all its biological claims.
neurips-2009-know-thy-neighbour-a-normat.tldr: The paper proposes that synaptic depression helps estimate a neighboring neuron’s membrane potential from spikes and derives testable biological predictions.

paragraphs: Approximating a complex probability distribution with simpler components is useful in tasks such as variational inference and classification. This paper focuses on mixtures of tree distributions. Such mixtures can be learned using an EM algorithm that minimizes KL divergence, but the quality of the outcome depends strongly on the trees used to initialize the procedure.

The authors propose selecting an initial collection that attempts to cover the observed distribution broadly. They express this goal through alpha-divergence with alpha equal to infinity and formulate it using fractional covering. The resulting sequential algorithm is convergent and requires solving a convex program at each iteration, providing a structured way to build the initial mixture.

Compared with previous methods, the approach produces significantly smaller tree mixtures with similar or better accuracy. This result links careful initialization to a more compact representation without a reported loss of predictive quality in the comparisons. The authors also demonstrate the method by learning pictorial structures for face recognition, showing how the distribution-approximation strategy can support a concrete visual recognition application.
neurips-2009-learning-a-small-mixture-of.tldr: A coverage-oriented initialization method learns smaller mixtures of tree distributions while retaining similar or better reported accuracy.

paragraphs: Freehand sketch recognition must cope with messy marks and differences in how people draw the same symbol. This paper proposes a framework that uses both the visual appearance of a symbol and its relationships with surrounding symbols. The aim is to make recognition more reliable when local drawing quality or style makes appearance alone difficult to interpret.

The framework combines a rich representation of low-level visual information with a graphical model of higher-level relationships. These components form a joint model of appearance and context. This allows evidence about neighboring symbols to contribute to recognition alongside the marks themselves, connecting local visual interpretation with the organization of the diagram.

The authors evaluate the method on molecular diagrams and electrical circuit diagrams, reporting significantly improved recognition performance. They attribute greater accuracy and robustness to reduced sensitivity to noise and drawing variation. The two application domains demonstrate the usefulness of the combined approach across different kinds of structured sketches. The main contribution is the integration of detailed appearance information and contextual relationships within one recognition framework.
neurips-2009-learning-from-neighboring-s.tldr: Combining symbol appearance with graphical context improves recognition of messy molecular and electrical circuit sketches.

paragraphs: Sparse image representations describe an image using a limited selection of elements from a learned dictionary. This paper develops a nonparametric Bayesian approach that learns the dictionary and infers an appropriate size for it. The method is applied to denoising, filling in missing image information, and reconstruction in compressive sensing.

A beta-process prior supports dictionary learning, while a Dirichlet process and a probit stick-breaking process are considered for capturing structure within an image. The dictionary can be learned directly from the image being processed. Training images can contribute when available, but the method does not require them. It also accommodates unknown noise variance and noise that varies across the image.

The authors explain that sequential inference can be used to scale the approach to large images. They present example results using both Gibbs sampling and variational Bayesian inference, alongside comparisons with state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution brings several forms of flexibility into one modeling approach: adapting dictionary size, using internal image structure, estimating noise, and allowing learning without a separate training collection.
neurips-2009-non-parametric-bayesian-dic.tldr: A Bayesian sparse-image model infers dictionary size, can learn directly from an image, and accommodates unknown spatially varying noise.

paragraphs: When objects overlap, the visible image depends both on which objects are present and on which ones are in front. This paper builds that distinction into a probabilistic generative model. One set of latent variables represents object presence, while another represents depth order, determining how the modeled positions and appearances combine into an image.

The goal is to learn object parameters from unlabeled images containing occlusion. Exact maximum-likelihood learning is intractable, so the authors develop approximations to Expectation Maximization. Their tractability depends on training images containing only a small number of objects on average. This condition makes learning feasible while retaining an explicit account of objects hiding parts of one another.

Numerical experiments show recovery of the correct object parameters. Tests with colored bars and more realistic data also show successful extraction of the underlying image-generating components, while standard bars experiments compare favorably with recent component-extraction methods. The contribution connects occlusion modeling with unsupervised discovery of multiple causes, showing how depth ordering can be incorporated into learning the objects that produce an image.
neurips-2009-occlusive-components-analys.tldr: An unsupervised model learns overlapping objects and their depth ordering using tractable approximations when images contain few objects on average.

paragraphs: This paper studies multiple kernel learning when kernels belong to distinct components and every component is assumed to matter for the task. That organization calls for two different preferences: combining information across components while selecting among kernels within each component. The authors encode these preferences through a mixed-norm regularizer motivated by applications such as object categorization.

The formulation uses an infinity-norm regularizer to encourage combinations at the component level and an L1 regularizer to encourage sparsity inside each component. Although previous attempts produced nonconvex problems, this formulation is convex, though nonsmooth. The authors develop an efficient mirror-descent procedure that optimizes over a product of simplexes, matching the grouped structure of the kernel choices.

Experiments on real datasets indicate that the formulation is well suited to object categorization. The mirror-descent algorithm also requires less computational effort than state-of-the-art kernel-learning solvers such as simpleMKL in the reported comparisons. The contribution combines a task-specific structural assumption with a convex formulation and an optimization method designed for its constraints.
neurips-2009-on-the-algorithmics-and-app.tldr: A convex mixed-norm formulation combines essential kernel groups while selecting within groups, with an efficient mirror-descent solver.

paragraphs: Choosing advertisements or ranking information sources involves interactions among the selected items. Redundant choices contribute less additional value, creating diminishing returns. This paper formalizes such problems as repeated assignments of items to positions, with each arriving objective described by a monotone submodular function. The formulation captures both placement decisions and the reduced benefit of overlapping choices.

The authors develop an efficient algorithm and analyze it within the no-regret framework. Their theoretical guarantee gives a performance ratio converging to the optimal constant of 1−1/e. This is an approximation guarantee for the stated online assignment problem, connecting repeated decision-making with the diminishing-returns structure of its objectives.

The algorithms are evaluated on two web applications: advertisement allocation with submodular utilities and dynamically ranking blogs to detect information cascades. These applications illustrate why value must be assessed jointly across selected items rather than independently for each item. The contribution is a general assignment-learning method with a strong asymptotic performance guarantee, together with empirical evaluations in two settings that motivate the mathematical formulation.
neurips-2009-online-learning-of-assignme.tldr: An efficient online assignment algorithm handles diminishing returns and achieves a performance ratio converging to the optimal constant 1−1/e.

paragraphs: Computing feature expectations in large models can involve expensive dynamic programs. Pruning speeds up this computation by skipping parts of the program, but using a single fixed pruning mask introduces bias. This paper proposes varying the mask through a randomized sequence so that computational savings can be combined with a principled treatment of the resulting approximation.

The masks are generated using auxiliary-variable Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. This supplies theoretical convergence guarantees for the approach. Each mask can skip substantial portions of the underlying dynamic program, making the method especially appealing for algorithms with high computational degree. The randomization is therefore part of an inference procedure with an analysis, rather than simply an arbitrary choice of discarded computations.

Experiments on bilingual parsing show that bias decreases as more masks are incorporated. The method also outperforms fixed tic-tac-toe pruning in the reported evaluation. These findings illustrate the intended tradeoff: individual computations remain pruned, while accumulating information across masks improves the estimate. The contribution links the speed benefits of pruning with a sampling-based route toward more accurate expectations.
neurips-2009-randomized-pruning-efficien.tldr: MCMC-generated pruning masks accelerate expectation calculations, with convergence guarantees and decreasing empirical bias as more masks are used.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor search looks for the data points closest to a query, but exact search becomes computationally expensive in high dimensions. Distance-based approximation can provide large speedups while weakening the ordering information that makes a neighbor useful. This paper focuses on accuracy expressed through rank: where a returned result falls in the ordering of distances.

The authors introduce a simple, practical algorithm that lets users directly control rank-based search accuracy while retaining large speedups over exact search. This changes the approximation target from closeness in distance value to closeness in the neighbor ordering. The distinction matters when the purpose of retrieval depends on returning highly ranked neighbors.

Experiments on high-dimensional datasets show that the algorithm often produces faster and more accurate results than the best-known distance-approximate method, with much more stable behavior. The reported advantage is empirical and qualified by how often it occurs. The central contribution is a controllable rank-oriented approximation that aligns the search criterion with ordering quality while addressing the computational cost of high-dimensional retrieval.
neurips-2009-rank-approximate-nearest-ne.tldr: A rank-controlled nearest-neighbor algorithm retains large search speedups and often improves accuracy and stability over distance-based approximation.

paragraphs: This paper introduces skill chaining, a method for discovering skills in reinforcement learning problems with continuous domains. Its organizing idea is to build chains of skills that lead toward a reward delivered at the end of a task. The connection among skills is central: discovery is directed toward assembling a route to the task’s rewarded outcome.

The approach gives skill discovery a task-oriented structure. A discovered skill contributes as part of a chain whose eventual destination is the end-of-task reward. This makes the relationship between skills and the overall objective explicit. The method is presented for continuous domains, placing the construction of these connected skills within that reinforcement learning setting.

The authors demonstrate experimentally that the resulting skills provide performance benefits in a challenging continuous domain. This supports the usefulness of skill chaining in the evaluated problem. The stated finding concerns the benefit of the skills the method creates, linking the proposed chain-building idea to improved task performance. The contribution is therefore both a method for organizing skill discovery and an experimental demonstration that its discovered skills can help an agent.
neurips-2009-skill-discovery-in-continuo.tldr: Skill chaining discovers connected skills leading to an end-of-task reward and demonstrates performance benefits in a challenging continuous domain.

paragraphs: Extensive games model interactions among multiple agents, but many interesting games are too large to solve directly. A common strategy is to simplify the original into a manageable abstract game, solve that version, and use its strategy in the original. The quality of the resulting strategy depends partly on what the abstraction allows it to express.

The paper notes that strategies from larger abstractions have tended to outperform those from smaller abstractions in computer poker competitions. Larger abstract games offer more expressive strategy spaces, but require solving larger problems. Strategy grafting introduces a way to compute more expressive strategies without increasing the size of the abstract games that must be solved.

The authors demonstrate the approach experimentally in both small and large games and provide a theoretical justification for the resulting improvement. Its significance is the separation between strategy expressiveness and the size of an individual abstraction that needs solving. This offers a way to improve strategies for large games while continuing to work with abstract games of manageable size.
neurips-2009-strategy-grafting-in-extens.tldr: Strategy grafting computes more expressive game strategies without requiring larger abstract games to be solved.

paragraphs: Finding a high-scoring configuration in a large relational factor graph is difficult because explicitly representing all hypotheses can cause exponential growth. Sampling methods can also become trapped when reaching a better solution requires first moving through lower-scoring configurations. This paper uses reinforcement learning to identify such temporarily unfavorable moves when they lead to better MAP solutions.

The method treats factor-graph parameters as a log-linear function approximator and learns them through temporal-difference learning. Inference on held-out data then executes the resulting policy. This changes the training objective from maximizing the likelihood of the training data to learning behavior that guides the search through configurations, including useful downward jumps.

Gradient updates require computing only factors near variables changed by an action, avoiding marginal computations entirely. On a complex joint ontology-alignment model, the authors report new state-of-the-art results and a 48 percent reduction in error relative to the previous state of the art in that domain. The result shows how learning the inference policy can improve both the practicality of search and the quality of its outcomes in the evaluated application.
neurips-2009-training-factor-graphs-with.tldr: Temporal-difference learning trains factor-graph search policies to make useful downward moves, yielding a reported 48 percent error reduction on ontology alignment.
